lessons.title: os meses — the gods and numbers of the calendar
lessons.gloss: the months — Roman gods, emperors, and the numbers 7–10

needs: your eyes for one table that cannot be read aloud
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes for one table that cannot be read aloud. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The months, taken apart until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: The Portuguese months are the Roman procession of gods and Caesars, worn down the Portuguese way. And two things you know pay off: março is the war-god, and setembro–dezembro are the Latin numbers 7–10.

There is a table here I cannot read to you — 4 columns and 12 rows, and it has more columns than can be held in the ear at once. Its columns are: Portuguese, from Latin, who / what, Spanish twin. Come back and look at it when you have stopped.
Portuguese tells: janeiro/fevereiro kept the -eiro ending ( from -arius, the same suffix in feira), and setembro/dezembro echo the numbers sete/dez you learned. Two payoffs:
março = Mars. The war-god's month, the same Mars behind English March.
setembro…dezembro = 7…10. Still the Latin numbers, because the Roman year began in March; then julho (Julius) and agosto (Augustus) were inserted and pushed the count down two.

segments.instruction: the twelve — "janeiro, fevereiro, março … novembro, dezembro"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the twelve — "janeiro, fevereiro, março … novembro, dezembro"]

segments.text: Which god is março named for? (Mars, the war-god.) Why is dezembro Latin for "ten"? (The Roman year began in March.) Which two months honour real people? (Julho — Julius; agosto — Augustus.) Next: the estações, the seasons.

lessons.title: as estações — the seasons, and a shifting summer
lessons.gloss: the seasons — and verão, a "summer" that came from "spring"

segments.text: Four seasons — and a small mystery in one of them. Portuguese's word for summer, verão, didn't come from a "heat" word like French été. It grew out of the word for spring. Here's how.

utterances: Portuguese: a primavera (spring). from Latin: prīma vēra. literally: "first spring / first green" (prima + ver "spring").
Portuguese: o verão (summer). from Latin: vēranum (tempus). literally: "the spring-like / warm season" ( from vēr "spring"!)
Portuguese: o outono (autumn). from Latin: autumnus. literally: "autumn" (ct/tumn becomes ut: autumnus becomes outono).
Portuguese: o inverno (winter). from Latin: hibernum. literally: "the wintry season" (cousin of hibernate).

segments.text: The twist is in the first two, both born from Latin vēr, "spring":
primavera = prima + ver: "the first spring / first green" — the year's opening season (shared with Spanish and Italian).

verão from vēranum, which meant "spring-like, of the growing season." Warmth crept forward on the calendar, and the word slid with it — so Portuguese's "summer" literally grew out of "spring." (Spanish did the same: verano.)
And outono from autumnus shows a familiar Portuguese move: the au…t smoothed to ou, the same softening you saw in oito and noite.

segments.instruction: "a primavera, o verão, o outono, o inverno"

segments.instruction: the twist — "verão from veranum from ver (spring): summer from spring"

segments.text: Name the four Portuguese seasons. (Primavera, verão, outono, inverno.) What's surprising about verão's origin? (It comes from vēr "spring" — the summer-word grew out of the spring-word.) What does primavera literally mean? ("First spring / first green.") Next chapter builds on this toward family and food.
